text: Salmonella survives 4–5 years in water, soil, dust, and shaded moist areas, so hygiene around the homestead and village is key to control. Presentation ranges from apparently healthy carrier animals to acute illness: high fever, and in adults severe, foul-smelling diarrhea with varying blood, mucus, and shreds of gut lining; abortion can occur; chronic cases (following an acute episode) show intermittent fever with persistent watery diarrhea, progressive dehydration, and weight loss. In calves 2–12 weeks old (especially those that missed colostrum): high fever, profuse yellow diarrhea (with or without blood/mucus flecks), rapid dehydration, and death within 24–48 hours. Treatment: rehydration is an emergency priority, as with E. coli; antibiotic effectiveness is uncertain since Salmonella develops resistance quickly (it's generally resistant to Tetracyclines already) — TMP+Sulfa, Colistin+Ampicillin, or Enrofloxacin can be tried, with treatment lasting at least 6 days. Diet-related (occasional) diarrhea: sometimes the only sign is watery feces with no other illness, usually from a feeding fault — a sudden feed change, heavy intake of young grass at the start of the rainy season, or old/decaying/fermenting feed (corn, rice bran). Treatment: introduce new grass or feed gradually, keep cattle under shelter with good-quality straw, and remove any soiled feed.
